s0: Welcome to the dojo. I am Sensei Shell. You already know how to run Claude Code. Today, we learn to run it well. Twenty-two short lessons, seven belts. Every lesson has something to click, press, or sort, so use your hands. Bow, and we begin.
s1: Everything in Claude Code bends around one rule. The context window fills up, and as it fills, quality drops. Every message, every file read, every command output costs space. Feed the window with the buttons on the left, then try the three ways to make room.
s2: Settings live in layers. Strongest first: your organization's managed settings, then command line flags, then project local, then shared project, then your user file. List keys like permissions allow merge across files instead of replacing each other. Click a layer, then sort the three scenarios. Run /status to see what actually loaded.
s3: Permissions are your biggest productivity lever. Press Shift+Tab to cycle modes. Manual asks before every edit and command. Accept edits lets file changes flow. Plan mode reads and thinks, but touches nothing. Auto lets a classifier review actions, so only risky ones interrupt you. Try an action in each mode.
s4: Match the model and effort to the task. Switch models without losing your prompt using Option+P, or Alt+P elsewhere. Use /effort to set how hard it thinks, and Option+O toggles fast mode. Typos deserve a light touch. Gnarly multi-file work deserves a plan and more effort. Drag the slider.
s5: CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session. Keep it under two hundred lines. For each line, ask: would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it. Sort these eight lines into keep or cut.
s6: Now the memory map. Run /init to draft a starter CLAUDE.md. Pull in other files with at-imports. Put topic rules in .claude/rules, and scope them to file paths so they load only when needed. Claude also keeps auto memory notes of its own. One warning: CLAUDE.md is advice, not enforcement. To guarantee behavior, use a hook.
s7: Time to train your hands. I will call a move. Press the real keys, or click the keycap if your browser fights you. Stop Claude with Esc. Rewind with Esc twice. Cycle modes with Shift+Tab. Edit your prompt in your editor with Ctrl+G. Search history with Ctrl+R. Go.
s8: Slash commands are your control panel. Clear between unrelated tasks. Compact with a focus. Rewind to any checkpoint. Ask a side question with /btw, and it never enters your history. Browse the deck, filter by category, and flip any card.
s9: Specific beats vague. Give Claude a way to check its own work, scope the task, point to existing patterns, and describe the symptom, not just the wish. Use @ to mention files, paste screenshots, and pipe in logs. Click a vague prompt to sharpen it.
s10: The workflow that avoids solving the wrong problem: explore, plan, implement, commit. Enter plan mode with Shift+Tab, let Claude read, and press Ctrl+G to edit the plan yourself. But if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan and just ask.
s11: Five traps catch almost everyone. The kitchen sink session. Correcting again and again. A bloated CLAUDE.md. Trusting without verifying. Endless exploration. Each has a fix, and most start with /clear or a smaller scope. Read the symptom, choose the fix.
s12: Claude Code has many extension points, and each one has a job. Hooks run every time, with no exceptions. Skills load on demand. Subagents keep research out of your context. MCP connects outside tools. Plugins bundle them. Match each need to the right tool.
s13: Once one session is smooth, multiply it. Worktrees give parallel sessions their own checkouts. A writer and a reviewer in fresh contexts catch more. Claude -p runs headless in scripts. And /batch fans a change across many subagents. Pick a mode and watch the lanes.
s14: This is the playground. A pretend terminal, safe to break. Try /status, /context, /compact, /clear, and /model. Try a bang command, or mention a file with at. Press Shift+Tab to cycle modes. Watch the context meter. Try at least six moves.
s15: Final trial. Eight questions. Pass with six and you earn the black belt, plus a cheat sheet to keep. Remember, productivity is not typing faster. It is managing context, verifying work, and letting the right tool do each job. Well done, student.
s16: Two different lists, two different scopes. The resume picker, from /resume, shows sessions for your current worktree. Press Ctrl+W to widen to every worktree of this repo, or Ctrl+A for every project on your machine. The left arrow on an empty prompt is something else. It sends this session to the background and opens agent view, which lists background sessions across all your projects. Name sessions so you can find them. Try both.
s17: Want two features in one repo at once? Give each its own worktree. Run Claude with the worktree flag and a name, once per terminal. Claude creates a checkout under .claude/worktrees on its own branch, so edits never collide. And yes, it manages the worktree for you. A clean one is removed when you exit. If there is work in it, you choose to keep or remove it. Step through it.
s18: Sometimes you need a detour. For a quick question, use /btw. It sees the whole session, uses no tools, and never enters your history. To try another approach, run /branch. You switch into a copy and the original stays resumable. Run /fork to copy the conversation into a background session while you keep working here. And while Claude works, just type. Your message queues, and Ctrl+Enter sends it now. Match each situation to the move.
s19: Set up your terminal once. On a Mac, turn on Option as Meta, or the Option shortcuts do nothing. In VS Code or Cursor, run /terminal-setup for Shift+Enter. To know when Claude needs you, Ghostty, Kitty and iTerm send desktop notifications. Elsewhere, set the terminal bell, or add a Notification hook that plays a sound. To look at files, use /diff for your changes, Ctrl+O for the transcript, Ctrl+G for your editor, and bang commands for anything else.
s20: Here is a feature that touches billing, notifications, and the API. Do it all in one window, and file reads swamp your context. Instead, interview first, write a spec, and start fresh. Then ask three subagents to research one module each, in parallel. Only their summaries come back. Implement in the main session, and have a reviewer subagent check the diff in a fresh context. Toggle each step and watch the meters.
s21: Here is a sensible starting kit. In user settings: allow rules for safe commands, deny rules for secrets, and a notification. In your global CLAUDE.md: only your personal habits. In each project CLAUDE.md: commands, style and gotchas, kept short. Ignore the worktrees folder in git. Toggle the pieces, copy what you like, then run /doctor to check your work.
